title: Strings
subtitle: f-strings, methods, slicing, and text processing
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Almost every program deals with text — user input, file content, API responses, log messages. Raw string handling is tedious without the right tools.
whyItExists.solution: Python strings are rich objects with 40+ built-in methods. f-strings make formatting clean. split/join/strip handle common text processing tasks elegantly.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time you process text. Parsing input, building messages, cleaning data, working with file content.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For complex pattern matching, use the re module. For large text processing, consider generators to avoid loading everything in memory.

explainModes.beginner: Python strings have a toolbox of methods — upper() makes text UPPERCASE, lower() makes it lowercase, strip() removes spaces from the ends, split() cuts a string into a list of parts.
explainModes.simple: Strings are immutable — methods return new strings, not modified originals. Key methods: upper/lower, strip/lstrip/rstrip, split/join, replace, find/index, startswith/endswith, in (membership), count, format/f-strings. Multiline with triple quotes. Raw strings: r'C:\Users\...'.
explainModes.standard: String indexing and slicing work the same as lists — strings are sequences. str.encode() converts to bytes; bytes.decode() back. Template strings (string.Template) for safe substitution. str.format_map() with dicts. str.translate() with str.maketrans() for character replacement tables. String interning: Python automatically interns short strings.
explainModes.technical: Python 3 strings are Unicode (UTF-8 compatible). str is immutable — every 'modification' creates a new object. For building strings in a loop, use a list + ''.join() — it's O(n) vs string concatenation's O(n²). str.format() is older but still common. bytes vs str: files opened in binary mode give bytes, text mode gives str. codecs for encoding handling.
explainModes.deepDive: Python's string interning interns strings that look like identifiers. sys.intern() forces interning for large sets of repeated strings. textwrap module for wrapping/indenting text. difflib for computing differences between strings. Levenshtein distance for fuzzy matching. unicodedata for Unicode property lookups. str.casefold() for case-insensitive comparison (handles ß→ss etc.).

content.code:
# Single, double, or triple quotes
name = 'Prashant'
quote = "It's easy"
essay = '''This is a
multiline string'''

# f-strings (Python 3.6+) — most modern way
age = 28
print(f'Name: {name}, Age: {age}')    # Name: Prashant, Age: 28
print(f'{name!r}')                     # 'Prashant' (repr)
print(f'{3.14159:.2f}')               # 3.14 (2 decimal places)
print(f'{1000000:,}')                  # 1,000,000 (thousands separator)
print(f'{"hello":^20}')               # centered in 20 chars
print(f'{42:08d}')                     # 00000042 (zero-padded)

# Raw strings — no escape processing
path = r'C:\Users\Prashant\Documents'
print(path)   # C:\Users\Prashant\Documents

text = '  Hello, World!  '

# Case
print(text.upper())          # '  HELLO, WORLD!  '
print(text.lower())          # '  hello, world!  '
print(text.title())          # '  Hello, World!  '

# Whitespace
print(text.strip())          # 'Hello, World!' (both ends)
print(text.lstrip())         # 'Hello, World!  ' (left only)
print(text.rstrip())         # '  Hello, World!' (right only)

# Search
print('World' in text)       # True
print(text.find('World'))    # 9 (index), -1 if not found
print(text.startswith(' '))  # True
print(text.endswith('!  '))  # True
print(text.count('l'))       # 3

# Modify (returns NEW string)
print(text.replace('World', 'Python'))
print(text.strip().split(', '))   # ['Hello', 'World!']

# Join — opposite of split
words = ['Hello', 'World']
print(', '.join(words))      # Hello, World
print('-'.join(['a','b','c']))  # a-b-c

# Check content
print('123'.isdigit())       # True
print('abc'.isalpha())       # True
print('abc123'.isalnum())    # True

questions.question: What does 'hello'.upper() return?
options: It modifies the original string to 'HELLO'
It raises an error — strings are immutable
questions.explanation: Python strings are immutable — methods never modify the original. upper() returns a NEW string with all characters uppercased. You must assign the result: name = name.upper().

faq.q: How do I efficiently build a string in a loop?
faq.a: Don't use += in a loop (O(n²) — creates a new string each time). Instead: collect parts in a list, then join: parts = []; for x in items: parts.append(str(x)); result = ', '.join(parts). This is O(n).

faq.q: What is the difference between find() and index()?
faq.a: Both search for a substring. find() returns -1 if not found. index() raises ValueError if not found. Use find() when absence is expected; use index() when absence is an error.
